analysis.one_liner: Pays dairy farmers to sell surplus cows to shrink milk supply and raises the government's milk price floor.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Vermont's two senators in May 1991, the bill received one Senate Agriculture Committee hearing and died in committee, never reaching a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Agriculture Department to buy up dairy cows and heifers from milk producers until U.S. milk production dropped by at least 5 billion pounds, with the goal of lifting farm milk prices. It would have raised the government's milk price support from $10.10 to $11.10 per hundredweight starting July 1991, though it required producers to give that increase back through a price reduction starting in 1992. It also created a fund to compensate beef producers who sold beef during a brief price dip in 1986, sent leftover funds to refugee assistance, and ordered a study of exporting dairy cattle. The program authority would have expired at the end of 1991.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers, especially in surplus milk regions, would gain twice over: the government buys their surplus cows, and the price floor for the milk they sell rises by $1 per hundredweight. Beef producers gain from a compensation fund for 1986 sales and from federal beef purchases designed to keep the cow buyout from depressing beef prices.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of Agriculture must purchase enough lactating cows and heifers from milk producers to cut U.S. milk production by at least 5 billion pounds, concentrating on surplus regions.
The milk price support rate rises from $10.10 to $11.10 per hundredweight for the second half of 1991, raising the floor under what dairy farmers receive.
Beef producers who sold beef between March 31 and April 11, 1986, when prices were temporarily lowered, can apply for compensation from a fund built from proceeds of the cattle purchases.
To keep the cow buyout from depressing beef prices, the Secretary may buy beef off the domestic market and transfer it for emergency food aid overseas.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay through higher milk prices as supply is pulled out of the market and the support floor rises. Taxpayers fund the beef purchases and the cattle purchase program, drawn from federal Commodity Credit Corporation savings. Milk producers themselves must give back the 1991 support increase through a mandated price reduction starting January 1, 1992.

drawbacks.text: Raising the milk support floor and shrinking supply works by raising retail milk prices, a cost that falls on every household that buys milk, including low-income families.

The bill's own offset erases much of the benefit: starting January 1, 1992, producers must accept a price reduction large enough to cancel out the 1991 support increase, so the gain is largely temporary.
The cattle purchase program was set to terminate on December 31, 1991, giving it a very short window even if enacted in 1991.

Paying farmers to sell cows to reduce production is a costly way to handle surplus; the funds for beef purchases and the $500,000 export study come from federal accounts, an expense an honest supporter would have to defend.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, if temporary, income help to dairy farmers in surplus regions, and the refund mechanism in 1992 shows its authors knew the price increase was not sustainable. But its main tool — cutting supply to raise prices — directly raises costs for consumers, and the beef compensation fund addresses a five-year-old price dip at federal expense. The consumer cost and short sunset limit made it a hard sell beyond dairy-state supporters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, got a single hearing in May 1991, and the committee never reported it out, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeffords introduced the bill with Sen. Leahy on May 17, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The committee held hearings on the bill on May 22, 1991, printed as S.Hrg. 102-479.
No further action was recorded; the bill never reached the Senate floor and expired with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Milk consumers and taxpayers are better off because the bill died, since it would have raised milk prices and spent federal money on a cattle buyout and a beef compensation fund. Dairy farmers seeking higher price supports came out behind.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: Chairman, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill and, as committee chair, held a hearing on it in May 1991; the committee never reported it to the floor.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on May 22, 1991, but never scheduled a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; sponsorship was bipartisan, with a Republican lead sponsor from Vermont, a Democratic co-introducer from Vermont, and one Democratic cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill buys up surplus cows and raises the price floor for milk, lifting farm income — but the mechanism works by shrinking milk supply and raising the retail price every household pays for milk.
The bill shields beef prices from the cow buyout through federal purchases and pays producers for a 1986 price dip from a federal fund, with the cost borne by taxpayers.
The bill funds a study of exporting heifers and lactating cows, which could open export markets for sellers of dairy cattle.
